title: Why are Gymnasts so FREAKY?
summary: NH explains how artistic gymnastics produces huge arms, abs, forearms and lats. The causes are straight-arm loading in stretched positions, constant tension, high grip and core demands, and years of training from childhood. He warns that copying gymnasts is unrealistic, since they also lift weights and are small and very lean. His takeaways are lengthened-position loading, constant tension, calisthenics and upper-limb loading.
claims: Artistic gymnastics is an upper body sport; most of the power comes from the limbs and torso, and six different apparatus push the whole body
Rings strength moves such as the iron cross or full planche must be held for at least 2 seconds to count
Gymnasts' huge biceps come from resisting elbow flexion while fully stretched, holding the whole bodyweight on straight arms
Gymnastics is the anti-powerlifting: instead of finding the most mechanically advantageous technique, gymnasts must hold the hardest positions because of aesthetic criteria
Most gymnastics positions keep the arms straight or externally rotated and supinated, so biceps and triceps stay under constant tension
The pommel horse builds the triceps because the arms support full bodyweight the whole time while tension switches rapidly between arms; try holding an L-sit from the floor to feel it
Gymnastics began in ancient Greece mixing training with philosophy; the Romans made it purely military, and German educators revived it after the defeats by Napoleon
Parallel bars require shoulders strong enough to support the body and mobile enough for full in-socket rotations that would injure most bodybuilders
Unlike bodybuilding reps, which allow rest at the top, gymnastics gives almost no respite, which is why abs and forearms are so developed
Constant core control in the air and positions like the L-sit, handstand and planche give elite gymnasts six-packs by default
Grip on rings and high bar plus constant elbow flexion build gymnasts' forearms
Getting very strong at pull-ups builds serious brachialis and biceps; gymnastics produces bigger arms than torso-dominant powerlifting
Gymnasts' lats come from constantly pulling themselves up plus adduction and abduction once up on the bars or rings
Elite gymnasts train 4-5 hours a day, 5-6 days a week, often from a young age, to build the neuromuscular patterns of six events
Stress fractures and ligament tears are common, and boys start later than girls because they need testosterone to handle the training
Hopping on rings for bigger biceps is silly; the hardest biceps skills take years to build, and you would be better off just doing curls
Rings are still useful for bodybuilding because straight-arm movements give an exceptional stretch; ring push-ups are great for the chest
The hype for gymnastics workouts for size comes from influencers who never trained the sport
Gymnasts also lift weights; biceps, triceps and shoulder isolation is part of their routine to grow those muscles without extra tendon stress
Most elite male gymnasts weigh 140-160 lb and are under 5'6 (Sam Mikulak about 141 lb, Donnell Whittenburg 160 lb), and they stay very lean year-round
Lesson one: exercises that safely load muscles in their lengthened position give great gains
Lesson two: constant tension through the whole range of motion produces substantial hypertrophy, while isometric holds are better for strength
Lesson three: do not dismiss calisthenics; the pec and lat stretch from bodyweight dips and pull-ups is hard to match
Lesson four: loading the upper limbs builds big biceps and triceps, so the spider physique is a matter of method, not fate
exercises: triceps and core under constant tension
